facts.value: CFR £126.625m at 31/03/2026 (GF £55.850m + HRA £70.775m). Gross external debt £92.304m (£91.764m fixed rate + £0.540m leases). Internal borrowing £34.321m. Percentage of CFR met by external debt fell from 81% at 31/03/2025 to 73% at 31/03/2026 — deliberate move to increased under-borrowing following £15m early PWLB repayment.

CFR £126.625m − external debt £92.304m = £34.321m internal borrowing — TIES EXACTLY to the £34.321m printed at Table 1 and (as '(Under)/Over funding of CFR') at Table 4. The £540k of leases sit inside the £92.304m external-debt figure per §4.1, so no separate 'other long-term liabilities' term is needed. No IFRS 16 restatement issue disclosed; the CFR movement table (Table 2) shows a small £175k new leases/IFRS16 line but it is within the reconciled totals.

TIES ON COUNT AND PRINCIPAL. PWLBtoday's file at 2026-03-31 shows 20 PWLB loans totalling £81,764,067 at a nominal principal-weighted 3.1713% (18 MATURITY + 2 EIP). Paper Table 9 (page 10): PWLB principal £81,764k, average life 31.62 years, 'Rate/Return' 2.82%. Principal and loan count match to the pound (ignoring rounding to £000). The 35bp gap on the weighted rate is the standard nominal-vs-effective-interest presentation gap seen at Redbridge and others.

facts.note: Email quotes '20 PWLB loans totalling £81,764,067' as the tie point. Weighted rate is not quoted in the email — the paper's 2.82% is the accounting rate and inviting a comparison would read as picking a fight over presentation. The 3.17% figure is only used internally.

facts.value: Eight PWLB loans totalling £15,000,000 principal repaid early on 21 November 2025 for a £5,794,442 net discount (38.63% overall). GF slice: £11,678,166 principal, (£5,310,829) discount = £6,367,337 net settlement, 45.5% overall discount rate. HRA slice: £3,321,834 principal, (£483,613) discount = £2,838,221 net settlement, 14.6% overall discount rate. £437,200 of annual interest saved on the eight loans (£291,622 GF + £145,578 HRA). The £5.8m discount credited to revenue/capital over a 10-year period; investment balances reduced by £9.2m.
facts.note: Rare in our library. Most councils don't take the discount — Warwickshire took £4.5m in 2024/25, Tameside took £2.8m, Leicestershire took £3.47m across five loans (the same exercise, run by different councils on different dates). NKDC's £5.79m at a 38.63% discount rate is a large and successful capture for a district. Paper does not identify which eight loans by ID, only the GF/HRA totals — so we cannot loan-by-loan reproduce the calculation the way we did for Leicestershire.

Of the 20, 17 sit below par and 3 above. Largest four indicative discounts: PW500342 EIP 2042-03-28 3.03% £30,329,067 (-£3,157,722); 173829 MAT 2070-03-20 1.76% £3,500,000 (-£2,139,467); 397981 MAT 2071-09-02 1.58% £2,000,000 (-£1,287,994); PW501332 EIP 2062-06-07 3.84% £6,840,000 (-£1,099,716).

facts.value: Three new external loans in year totalling £20m: £10m WMCA (West Midlands Combined Authority) drawn 16/07/2025, 3-year term, 4.10% (GF); £5m PWLB drawn 28/01/2026, 1-year maturity, 4.35% (GF); £5m PWLB drawn 28/01/2026, 1-year maturity, 3.95% (HRA). §7.6 rationale: 'These short-term loan periods were selected to allow interest rates to reduce in line with MUFG forecasts thus avoiding a long-term external loan on relatively high interest rates.'
facts.note: Dated, falsifiable strategy statement. On the paper's own comparators the 30y certainty fell from 6.20% (16/07/25) to 5.96% (28/01/26), so within the year the forecast partly delivered. Between 28/01/26 and 14/08/26 the long end moved sideways-to-up: today's 10y certainty 5.83% and 20y 6.38% against January's 5.31% and 5.87% — roughly +0.5 percentage points at both tenors.

facts.value: £17.086m of external debt matures within 12 months at 31/03/2026 — 18.6% of the £91.764m total. Composed of the two £5m PWLB 1-year maturity loans drawn 28/01/2026 (maturing 28/01/2027), plus £2.086m of scheduled PWLB EIP repayments and any residual liquidity items. The £10m WMCA 3-year loan sits in the 2-5 year bucket (matures 16/07/2028). Comparatives 31/03/2025: only £2.086m in the under-12-months bucket.
facts.note: The £10m at 4.15% weighted (5m at 4.35 + 5m at 3.95) is now inside the refinancing window on the paper's own certainty rates. At today's PWLB certainty (14/08/26) a 1-year is 4.95%; 5-year 5.34%; 10-year 5.83%.

facts.value: General Fund financing costs as % of net revenue stream: 5.12% in 2025/26, up from 4.49% in 2024/25 (£1,945k over £38,016k). HRA financing costs as % net revenue: 20.85% in 2025/26, up from 20.30% in 2024/25 (£4,180k over £20,046k). Both slightly rising; HRA typical for a stock-holding landlord.

Loans to wholly owned subsidiary Lafford Homes Ltd £40.818m at 31/03/2026 (up from £25.344m at 01/04/2025). Split: 25 investment loans (completed schemes) £19,978,962 with maturity dates 2027/28 to 2033/34, generating £860,178 interest in 2025/26; plus development loans £5,364,857 (2024/25 advances, £353,919 accrued) and £15,474,107 (2025/26 advances, £497,916 accrued). Development loans are short-term (3-5 years), interest accrued and payable when scheme completes and converts to an investment loan. Additional £2.350m cashflow facility current balance; total loan exposure £44.020m with further £17.576m of committed drawdowns available.

Table 13 proportionality indicators (current / committed): Total Exposure as % of Total Investments 64% / 94%; Total Exposure as % of Non-treasury Investments 90% / 97%; Exposure as % of CFR 77% / 88%; Contribution to Investment Income 50% / 64%. Paper text (page 15) states plainly: 'The proportionality indicators demonstrate that the Council's exposure to Lafford Homes is significant and highly concentrated, particularly in the context of non-treasury investments and the Council's overall borrowing position.'
facts.note: Unusually candid disclosure — two full pages of concentration analysis with the six-indicator table and the explicit narrative. Most districts we have read that lend heavily to their wholly-owned company do not publish this analysis. Worth noting in the email as unusual disclosure. Do not present as advice; the exposure sits outside PWLBtoday's PWLB data scope.

summary.text:
A well-structured district annual treasury outturn from a HRA-holding council. The headline is a £15m early repayment executed on 21 November 2025 that captured a £5.794m net discount at a 38.63% overall discount rate on eight PWLB loans (Table 7). GF slice was £11.68m at 45.5% discount, HRA slice £3.32m at 14.6% — a large, real transaction that most councils in our library have not tried. £437,200 of annual interest saved; the £5.8m discount credited to revenue/capital over ten years.

Loan-book ties to our file on count and principal exactly: 20 PWLB loans totalling £81,764,067 against Table 9's £81,764k. Weighted rate differs (ours 3.17% nominal; paper's 2.82% is the effective interest rate booked through accounts — the same presentation gap Redbridge and others show, not raised in the email as a discrepancy). Balance-sheet identity ties to the pound: CFR £126.625m − external debt £92.304m (£91.764m fixed + £0.540m leases) = £34.321m internal borrowing.

Two other things stand out. First, £17.086m of the £91.764m book sits in the under-12-months bucket, of which £10m is the two 1-year PWLB loans (£5m GF at 4.35% + £5m HRA at 3.95%) drawn 28 January 2026 and maturing 28 January 2027. §7.6 states plainly they were taken short 'to allow interest rates to reduce in line with MUFG forecasts.' Between January 2026 and 14 August 2026 the curve has moved slightly the other way (10y certainty 5.31% → 5.83%, 20y 5.87% → 6.38%). Second, the paper devotes two full pages to the Lafford Homes concentration risk — £44.020m of exposure, 90% of non-treasury investments, 77% of GF CFR, 50% of investment income — and explicitly labels it 'highly concentrated' (page 15). That level of candour on wholly-owned company exposure is unusual in the districts we have read.

officer.subject: Your November discount capture, and the shape of what remains
officer.body:
Dear Charlotte,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2025/26 annual treasury report that went to Resources Scrutiny on 13 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is well laid out, the Lafford Homes section in particular is more candid than most, and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

First, a proof of read that also proves our loan file is straight. Your Table 9 shows £81,764k of PWLB at 31 March 2026 with an average life of 31.62 years. Our file at the same date has 20 PWLB loans totalling £81,764,067 — the same number, to the pound, ignoring rounding to £000. The rate we carry is the principal-weighted nominal (3.17%); the 2.82% in your Rate/Return column is the effective interest rate booked through the accounts, which is a presentation difference rather than a disagreement about which loans are outstanding.

The part of the report that stands out is Table 7 and paragraph 7.2. Repaying £15m of PWLB on 21 November 2025 and capturing a £5.794m net discount — 45.5% on the General Fund slice, 14.6% on the HRA — is a real transaction that most councils in the library we have read this summer have not attempted. Warwickshire took £4.5m off in the same kind of exercise, Tameside £2.8m, Leicestershire £3.47m across five loans; your £5.794m sits at the top of that peer set, and £437,200 comes off the annual interest run-rate on top. It's the kind of thing that only happens if the treasury team and MUFG have the analysis in front of them at the moment the curve moves — and you had.

On the twenty remaining loans, our engine on the DMO's 14 August curve prices seventeen of them below par and three above, with a total indicative net discount of around £17.2m against £81.7m of live principal — roughly 21% of the book. The largest single indicative discount is on your PW500342 EIP loan (£30.3m, 3.03%, matures 2042), which alone shows about £3.2m of theoretical discount today. None of that is a quote — the DMO's own quote is the only binding one, and our engine models the DMO's curve rather than MRP or the accounting treatment or the replacement-cost cash-flow you would actually have to model to decide whether anything is worth doing. It is genuinely just to say the shape of what remains still carries substantial discount on today's curve, and the analysis you commissioned for the November exercise is exactly the kind that would tell you whether a further slice is worth revisiting.

One other observation. Your paragraph 7.6 is explicit that the two 1-year PWLB loans in January were taken short to allow interest rates to reduce in line with MUFG forecasts. Between the borrowing date and mid-August the ten-year certainty rate has moved from 5.31% to 5.83% and the twenty-year from 5.87% to 6.38%, so those forecasts have not delivered on that horizon so far. The £10m matures on 28 January 2027 and is inside its own refinancing window now; whichever way the curve moves between now and then, our loan-analysis and rate pages track it daily.

A standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway is becoming central to how treasury strategy is framed, and an interactive version tied to live rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. For a council with £34m of internal borrowing carrying real cost-of-carry against £68m of investments, the shape of that pathway is directly readable.

On training, three fit North Kesteven. PWLB break costs — mechanics and live calculator picks up directly from what you have just executed. Internal borrowing and the cost of carry is the framing under paragraph 7.9. Treasury management for councillors is written for the scrutiny your Resources Committee gives this, and free for members. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
